meta.title: Serbian A2 Elementary
meta.subtitle: 750 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Serbian → English (see the Serbian, recall the meaning) and English → Serbian (see an English meaning, recall the Serbian). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 750 words for an elementary learner, aligned to A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand sentences and frequently used expressions related to areas of most immediate relevance' — a learner here is able to manage simple, routine exchanges of information on familiar matters — personal and family information, shopping, the local area, work — and to describe in simple terms their background, their surroundings and what they immediately need. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no graded Serbian word list could be used, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 389 of the 750 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — relatives and the people around you, jobs and study, clothes, more food and cooking, the rooms and furniture of a home, the town and its services, travel and holidays, nature, the seasons and the compass, animals, health and the body, feelings and character, free time, sport and holidays, telling what happened when, the higher numbers and measures, and the everyday verbs of moving, dressing, cooking and doing — and the other 361 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Serbian, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. The Serbian is the standard of Serbia: Ekavian (млеко, време, леп, not the Ijekavian млијеко, вријеме, лијеп of Bosnia and Montenegro), and words Wiktionary marks as only Croatian or Bosnian are left out. Every headword is printed in Cyrillic, the official alphabet, with its accent marked as Wiktionary gives it (ку̏ћа, вре́ме), and again in the Latin alphabet beneath (kuća, vreme), since Serbian is read in both every day; the Serbian Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the letters, the two alphabets and the accent marks. The 401 nouns show their gender, their genitive and their plural; the 186 verbs show their aspect, imperfective or perfective, their ја and он forms and their past; and behind the All forms fold every noun's seven cases and every verb's present, future, past and imperative. Real example sentences come with 662 of the 750 words, three apiece for 538 of them, in Cyrillic with the Latin spelling beneath, the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender, aspect, accents and forms: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.

У овој фази светске историје, у Америци не постоји једна таква ствар као што је независна штампа. Ви то знате и ја то знам. Међу вама нема ни једног који се усуђује да напише своје искрено мишљење, и кад би га написао, већ унапред би знао да се то никада неће појавити у штампи. Ја сам добијао редовно своју плату како бих држао своје искрено мишљење изван новина за које радим. Многи од вас су такође слично плаћени за сличне ствари, и било ко од вас ко би био толико луд да пише оно што искрено мисли, нашао би се напољу, на улици, у потрази за неким другим послом. Да сам ја дозволио да се моје право мишљење појави само у једном издању новина за које радим, добио бих отказ с посла за мање од 24 часа. (...)
U ovoj fazi svetske istorije, u Americi ne postoji jedna takva stvar kao što je nezavisna štampa. Vi to znate i ja to znam. Među vama nema ni jednog koji se usuđuje da napiše svoje iskreno mišljenje, i kad bi ga napisao, već unapred bi znao da se to nikada neće pojaviti u štampi. Ja sam dobijao redovno svoju platu kako bih držao svoje iskreno mišljenje izvan novina za koje radim. Mnogi od vas su takođe slično plaćeni za slične stvari, i bilo ko od vas ko bi bio toliko lud da piše ono što iskreno misli, našao bi se napolju, na ulici, u potrazi za nekim drugim poslom. Da sam ja dozvolio da se moje pravo mišljenje pojavi samo u jednom izdanju novina za koje radim, dobio bih otkaz s posla za manje od 24 časa. (...)
There is no such thing, at this stage of the world’s history in America, as an independent press. You know it and I know it. There is not one of you who dare write your honest opinions, and if you did, you know beforehand that it would never appear in print. I am paid weekly for keeping my honest opinions out of the paper I am connected with. Others of you are paid similar salaries for similar things, and any of you who would be foolish as to write honest opinions would be out on the streets looking for another job. If I allowed my honest opinions to appear in one issue of my papers, before twenty-four hours my occupation would be gone. The business of the journalist is to destroy the truth, to lie outright, to pervert, to vilify, to fawn at the feet of Mammon, and to sell his country and his race for his daily bread. You know it and I know it, and what folly is this toasting an independent press? We are the jumping jacks, they pull the strings and we dance. Our talents, our possibilities and our lives are all the property of other men. We are intellectual prostitutes.
